A: Production-ready card-face typography and play-state readability: names, rules text, and stat chips read instantly at every zoom level.
Cohesive flat-graphic art language: the cards, divider, and field all speak one consistent vector style with no rendering-technique seams.
Clean, unambiguous play-grid geometry: the crisp divider beam, diamond node, and outlined empty slot keep the board structure perfectly legible.
B: Fully realized meadow environment: stream with banks, planted fence, flowers, rocks, and low-poly trees frame the field with believable depth, scale, and cozy warmth.
Superb ground/card integration: cards have edge thickness, decks and graves stack physically, and warm contact shadows plus light spill make cards sit ON the world rather than float over it.
Atmospheric, integrated divider and lighting: the crackling energy seam bleeds light into the grass, and a consistent golden-hour sun bathes the whole battlefield in a single believable light.

A: Replace the abstract dark-teal polygon clumps at the field edges with resolved environment props (shaded trees, rocks, flower clusters); in every corner crop they currently read as unfinished masking shapes, not a meadow.
Remove or drastically soften the heavy dark corner vignette; it muddies the olive ground into dirty gradients and fights the 'sunlit meadow' brief instead of framing it.
Give cards physical presence: add edge thickness, a visible stacked pile for deck/grave zones, and warmer, tighter contact shadows so cards stop floating on a flat color field.
Add ground micro-detail to the play surface (grass texture, scattered petals, mow-band variation, subtle noise); the flat mustard fill between cards reads as a UI background, not terrain.
Integrate the divider into the world: let its light spill onto the ground and introduce slight organic irregularity; the current perfectly straight beam reads as a plastic strip laid over the scene.
B: Pull back the global warm haze/bloom across the mid-field; it stains the center grass yellow and flattens contrast where the most important cards sit.
Tighten rendering crispness on card frames, badges, and aperture art; several faces go soft to the point of mush at full-field distance, hurting scan speed.
Boost empty-slot ghost outlines a step; they nearly vanish in the brightest grass (opponent middle slot especially), weakening play-grid legibility.
Lock a single sun vector for all cast shadows; deck stacks and face-up cards disagree slightly in shadow angle/length, which subtly breaks the otherwise excellent grounding.
Replace the glyph placeholder rules text with real typography and verify legibility at table zoom; the painterly text plates need a readability pass before the field language can be called shipped.

notes: Blind A/B verdict, field/staging criteria only. A is a flat vector render with strong graphic clarity and the best text readability of the two, but its environment framing is essentially unresolved: dark polygon clumps plus a heavy vignette stand in for scenery, the ground is an untextured mustard fill, and cards float with thin drop shadows. B is a warm painterly-low-poly meadow where every framing element (stream, fence, rocks, flowers, trees) is resolved, cards have thickness, stacks, and contact shadows that anchor them to the ground, and the divider is an organic light seam that belongs to the world. B wins all ten crops on battlefield criteria. Declared divergences respected: B's glyph placeholder card text and simple aperture scenes were not held against it for content, though text legibility is flagged as a real improvement item; A's missing HUD elements were ignored as out of scope. B's main risks are bloom-induced contrast loss and soft edges; A's card-face design system is its keepable asset.
